decisions.reconsider_when: The readable-target class covers the common applications well enough that a bounded automatic retry is safe for those targets specifically.

decisions.title: Recording display as a non-activating panel with provisional and final states distinguished
decisions.choice: An NSPanel with nonactivating and borderless style, status-bar level, joining all spaces, movable by background, ordered front without becoming key. Provisional text renders in a secondary style with a live label; the final transcript replaces it in the primary style with a brief change highlight. The waveform is drawn from a 10 ms RMS and peak envelope computed allocation-free on the capture thread. Failures appear as a row with a short reason and one action. Placement is stored as a fraction of the display's visible frame plus the display identifier, clamped to the primary display when either is gone.
decisions.rationale: The panel must never become key, since activating it would break the delivery latch that D-008 depends on. Provisional and final text are different artifacts, so they are shown differently instead of silently swapped, and the provisional stream is never persisted as a result. Fractional placement survives resolution and display changes, which is the usual failure of remembered window positions.

alternatives.option: A normal SwiftUI window
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard behavior and less AppKit; it activates the application and changes the frontmost application, breaking delivery targeting.

alternatives.option: Menu bar popover only
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra window; anchored to the menu bar so it cannot sit near where the user is typing, and it dismisses on outside clicks.

alternatives.option: Promote the provisional transcript as the final result
alternatives.tradeoff: Feels faster; delivers text produced from partial context as final, the confusion the requirement asks to prevent.

decisions.consequences: Panel focus and level behavior is AppKit-managed with SwiftUI content and needs its own tests. Users see text change when the final transcript arrives, which is highlighted instead of silent. When the scheduler denies the provisional pass, the panel shows preview paused in place of a stalled transcript.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measurement shows the provisional pass costs dropped buffers or final-transcript quality, in which case the preview degrades to waveform plus a voice-activity indicator.

decisions.title: Modes as versioned revisions with structured transformation contracts and a fail-closed validator
decisions.choice: Every mode, built-in or custom, carries a structured TransformationContract (allowed operations, an answersQuestions flag, a content bound expressed as a recall threshold or a citation requirement, and the languages its validator supports) alongside its free-form prompt. Revisions are content-addressed over prompt, formatting rules, contract and model selections, and runs pin a revision id. Generated output is checked against the contract in the run's language: interrogatives present in the normalized transcript survive in order unless answersQuestions is declared; expansion ratio stays under the mode's limit; content-word recall exceeds the threshold; no span of eight or more tokens appears that is present in the context block and absent from the transcript; sentences with no content-word support in the input are flagged. On failure the run retries once with a stricter instruction, then falls back to the normalized transcript, marked as a validator fallback. When the run's language has no validator pack for the mode, the generation stage is skipped and the normalized transcript is used, unless the user sets a per-mode override that is off by default and recorded on the result.
decisions.rationale: Prompt wording cannot enforce that a dictated question stays a question, particularly when context contains instruction-shaped text, and delimiter framing influences a model without constraining it. Making permitted transformations a machine-checkable property turns the requirement into a gate with a defined failure path. Custom modes need a structured contract precisely because their prompts are free-form, so the contract is a required field instead of something inferred from prose. Failing closed on an unvalidatable language keeps the multilingual promise of D-017 from quietly bypassing the gate. The claim stops there: these checks are necessary conditions and the adversarial corpus in verification is the standing test of how far they reach.

alternatives.option: Prompt instructions only, no validator
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and preserves whatever the model produces; the failure mode is a model answering a dictated question and the answer being pasted into a document.

alternatives.option: Infer permitted transformations from the custom prompt
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing extra for the user to fill in; the inference is itself a language-model judgment with the failure mode it is meant to catch.

alternatives.option: Validate with a second model asked whether the output is faithful
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches semantic drift lexical checks miss; costs a second generation pass on the latency path and inherits the same failure mode.

alternatives.option: Deliver unvalidated output for unsupported languages
alternatives.tradeoff: No degradation for multilingual users; the contract stops being enforced exactly where the user cannot check it themselves.

decisions.consequences: The custom mode editor cannot save a mode without a contract, which is friction the editor makes quick with presets. Thresholds need tuning against the fidelity corpus, and bad thresholds show up as frequent visible fallbacks. Languages ship with packs one at a time, so multilingual rewriting is limited by pack coverage instead of by model coverage, and the panel says which.
decisions.reconsider_when: Fallback rates stay high on correct outputs, the adversarial corpus finds a violation class that passes every check, or pack coverage becomes the binding limit on multilingual use.

decisions.title: Built-in mode set and their contracts
decisions.choice: Four read-only built-in modes, each with an explicit contract. Standard: punctuation, capitalization, optional disfluency removal, vocabulary substitution; no reordering, no summarizing, no answering. Email: Standard plus salutation and sign-off from a template, paragraph breaks, register adjustment, no new factual content, recall-bounded body. Note: adds list and heading structure, recall-bounded. Meeting notes: summarization permitted, bounded by a citation requirement where every bullet references a real segment range and uncited bullets are dropped. All four declare answersQuestions false. English packs ship first; other languages fall back per D-012 until their packs exist.
decisions.rationale: The specification asks for ordinary dictation plus task-specific output with permitted transformations specified per mode. Meeting notes is the one mode where summarization is the point, so recall cannot be its guard and a citation requirement fits what it is allowed to do.

alternatives.option: One configurable mode with toggles
alternatives.tradeoff: Less to explain; the contract dissolves into a toggle matrix that is hard to validate against.

alternatives.option: A larger built-in catalog
alternatives.tradeoff: More coverage out of the box; each mode needs its own fidelity corpus and rubric, and custom modes already cover these.

alternatives.option: Ship an assistant mode that answers dictated questions
alternatives.tradeoff: An obvious use of a local language model; it is the behavior the requirements single out as a hazard, so it would have to declare answersQuestions and be visibly distinct in the mode indicator.

decisions.consequences: Built-ins are read-only; customizing one duplicates it into a user mode carrying the same contract as a starting point, which keeps the built-in fidelity corpus meaningful. Four modes means four rubric corpora per shipped language.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users routinely duplicate a built-in to make the same edit, which is evidence the built-in should change.

decisions.title: Automatic mode selection: ordered rules, specificity tiebreak, latched at arming
decisions.choice: An ordered rule list evaluated at arming, first match wins, ordered by the user, with specificity as the tiebreak within equal priority (URL host plus path prefix, then host, then bundle identifier, then any). The selected mode is latched into the run manifest. A predicate whose input cannot be obtained does not match, and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies. The editor flags rules that can never fire because an earlier rule shadows them.
decisions.rationale: First match on a user-ordered list is the model people know from mail filters and makes conflict resolution inspectable. Treating an unobtainable predicate as a non-match keeps a missing permission from producing a wrong mode. Latching at arming means the mode cannot change under the user mid-sentence.

alternatives.option: Highest specificity wins regardless of order
alternatives.tradeoff: No shadowed rules; the user cannot temporarily override a specific rule with a general one.

alternatives.option: Re-evaluate continuously during capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Follows the user across windows; the mode could change mid-sentence and the run would no longer have one manifest.

alternatives.option: Infer the mode from what was said
alternatives.tradeoff: No rules to configure; requires recognition before mode selection, inverting the pipeline and making the current mode unpredictable.

decisions.consequences: The effective mode and whether it came from a rule or the fallback appear in the panel and menu bar for every run. Switching applications mid-recording keeps the mode chosen where the user started, consistent with the delivery latch. Browser URL availability varies and is enumerated per browser instead of assumed.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users regularly start recording, notice the wrong mode and cancel, which would argue for a mode change during capture before recognition begins.

decisions.title: Vocabulary as staged passes with a defined order around recognition and generation
decisions.choice: Four stages in fixed order. Recognition biasing puts selected terms in the decoder prompt slot, capped to the runtime limit, chosen by mode relevance and recency. Deterministic replacement over the recognition result applies ordered rules, longest match first, boundary-aware using ICU word segmentation for the run's language, case-preserving, non-overlapping, applied once with no cascading. Filler removal is a separate per-mode pass. After generation the replacement table is applied once more and the validator checks that vocabulary terms survived. Recognition and normalized results are both retained. For scripts without word spacing, replacement uses ICU segmentation where available and otherwise falls back to substring matching with a warning shown in the vocabulary editor.
decisions.rationale: The mechanisms fail differently and must not be conflated. Prompt biasing changes decoding probabilities and guarantees nothing, so the interface says so and never claims that adding a name makes it recognized. Deterministic replacement is exact and belongs on text. The post-generation pass exists because a language model will sometimes normalize an unusual proper noun back to a common word, and the user's spelling should win. Word boundaries are language-dependent, so the boundary rule names its mechanism instead of assuming spaces.

alternatives.option: Replacement only after generation
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass; the generation stage then reasons over text containing mis-recognized terms.

alternatives.option: Replacement only before generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler; a model that alters a name in its output goes uncorrected.

alternatives.option: Ask the language model to apply the vocabulary
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles inflection and context that literal matching misses; makes an exact user-specified substitution probabilistic, which is the property users want here.

alternatives.option: Cascading replacement to a fixpoint
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles chained rules; introduces order-dependent results and possible loops for a rarely needed benefit.

decisions.consequences: Two texts per run to store and show. The editor must explain that terms have one probabilistic effect and one exact effect. The prompt slot forces selection when the vocabulary is large, so the panel can show which terms were included.
decisions.reconsider_when: A runtime exposes real biasing or constrained decoding, which moves exact-name handling into recognition.

decisions.title: Context sources: sampled at arming, budget-bounded, digest-only retention, framed as data
decisions.choice: Three optional sources sampled in parallel at arming against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text, selection and window title through accessibility, capped at 4000 characters; one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition, opt-in; the first text item on the pasteboard, capped. Anything missing the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Retention defaults to digest, length and source kind; retaining text is opt-in per mode and deleted with the recording. In the prompt, context sits inside a per-run random delimiter, labeled reference material, with mode instructions before and the task restated after. Enforcement that context did not become instructions is the contract validator and its context n-gram check (D-012), with the fail-closed path as the bound on damage.
decisions.rationale: Sampling once at arming bounds cost and makes a run reproducible; continuous sampling would make the same recording produce different prompts depending on timing. Digest-only retention keeps the library from accumulating copies of unrelated documents and screens while still letting a reprocess report that the original context is gone. Framing reduces instruction-following on context text without preventing it, which is why the validator carries the requirement.

alternatives.option: Sample at generation time
alternatives.tradeoff: Fresher context and screen recognition off the latency path; by then the user has often switched windows, so the sample describes somewhere they no longer are.

alternatives.option: Retain full context text by default
alternatives.tradeoff: Reprocessing reproduces the original result exactly; the library accumulates screen and clipboard contents by default, a privacy posture the product should not adopt quietly.

alternatives.option: Continuous screen sampling during capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures what changed while speaking; sustained recognition cost and a much larger retention question.

decisions.consequences: Screen recognition may routinely miss the deadline on busy displays and is then absent and noted. Reprocessing a recording whose context was not retained produces a different result, and History shows why. Injection resistance is defense in depth backed by the corpus in verification.
decisions.reconsider_when: Screen context proves valuable enough that users want it reliably, which moves sampling off the arming path and makes the rewrite stage wait for it.

decisions.title: Languages: per-mode selection or detection, translation as a derived result of a named recognition
decisions.choice: Each mode sets recognition language to an explicit code or to auto. Auto uses the runtime's language identification with its probability; below threshold the run records undetermined, uses the mode's default language, and the panel says so. Translation to English is a separate declared operation producing a result whose derived_from_result_id names the exact recognition or normalized result it translated. Each model installation declares supported languages, labeled in the interface as declared by the publisher and unmeasured until an evaluation row exists.
decisions.rationale: Recognition quality and rewriting quality are different properties measured by different methods, so they are represented and evaluated separately. Naming the parent result is what makes translation provenance survive a second recognition of the same audio; without it, a translation of the first transcript looks equally like a translation of the second. Marking language support as declared keeps the product from promising coverage nobody measured.

alternatives.option: Always auto-detect
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to configure; short utterances and code-switching produce wrong detections and the user cannot pin a language they know.

alternatives.option: Translate by replacing the transcript
alternatives.tradeoff: One text per recording; the original wording is unrecoverable, breaking reprocessing and review.

alternatives.option: Translate as part of the rewrite
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass; translation and formatting become entangled and the validator cannot separate a translation error from a formatting one.

decisions.consequences: History shows several artifacts per recording and must make the parent of each obvious. A user-supplied model with an inaccurate manifest can overstate coverage, so the interface attributes the claim to the manifest. Rewriting in a language with no validator pack takes the fail-closed path from D-012, so multilingual recognition is broader than multilingual rewriting and the interface says which.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured detection accuracy on short utterances makes auto safe as the default, or a runtime provides per-segment language identification supporting code-switching within a recording.

decisions.title: One ingest port carrying timing and flow control, with a declared format matrix
decisions.choice: All sources implement AudioSource, emitting AudioFrame values that carry stream id, clock domain, presentation time, sequence number, discontinuity flag, native sample rate, channel layout and sample format. Conversion to the canonical 16 kHz mono Float32 recognition input is an explicit stage after the port. Consumers grant credit; a seekable source stops decoding when credit is exhausted, and a live source that overruns drops frames and records a discontinuity instead of buffering without bound. Credit extends across the service connection, so the window queue inside a service is bounded by the same accounting. Microphone via AVAudioEngine, system audio via ScreenCaptureKit, files via AVAssetReader in 30-second windows. Initial matrix: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v, mov. Extension: a DecoderProvider port with an opt-in external command-line decoder adapter, off by default, run inside the sandboxed decode service.
decisions.rationale: An untimestamped canonical buffer cannot express what meetings need, which is two native streams aligned by host time with drift and gaps visible, and it cannot express backpressure, which is what actually bounds memory end to end. Windowed decoding bounds the decoder; credit bounds the queue between decoder, converter and recognizer, including across the connection. RESEARCH notes whisper.cpp's example has input-format constraints, so an explicit decoding boundary is needed regardless of which runtime ships.

alternatives.option: Canonical untimestamped buffers
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest consumer code; meeting alignment and gap reporting have to travel around the abstraction, and flow control has nowhere to live.

alternatives.option: Separate live and seekable ports
alternatives.tradeoff: Each expresses its own timing and retry rules; orchestration, cancellation and conversion get duplicated between them.

alternatives.option: Decode whole files into memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest of all; a three-hour file at 16 kHz Float32 is roughly 700 MB before any model loads, which the requirements rule out.

alternatives.option: Bundle a general-purpose decoder
alternatives.tradeoff: Every format works out of the box; adds licensing obligations, binary size and a security update duty for a decoder parsing untrusted files.

decisions.consequences: Every source carries timing metadata even when it has one stream and no drift. Live overrun is a visible discontinuity in the recording instead of a silent gap. Canonical conversion discards content above 8 kHz for recognition, so imported originals are kept and meeting streams are sealed at native rate for later use.
decisions.reconsider_when: A speech runtime benefits from a higher input rate, or the credit mechanism proves unnecessary because every runtime consumes faster than any source produces.

decisions.title: Imports are copy-in and commit-late, leaving the source untouched
decisions.choice: Import opens the source read-only, copies it into the session directory, and records a security-scoped bookmark for provenance. The recording row commits only when the artifact is complete and readable. On any failure the session directory is removed and no row exists. Moving the original happens only after commit, as a step the user can decline.
decisions.rationale: A failed import leaves its source unchanged if the import path never opens the source for writing and never deletes it. Committing after the artifact is complete keeps a failure from leaving a History entry pointing at nothing.

alternatives.option: Reference the source in place
alternatives.tradeoff: No duplication; the library breaks when the user moves or deletes the file, and reprocessing later finds nothing.

alternatives.option: Transcode on import and discard the original
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller library and one decode path; discards information and makes reprocessing with a better decoder impossible.

alternatives.option: Create the row first and fill it in
alternatives.tradeoff: Progress visible immediately; a failure leaves a broken row for recovery to reason about.

decisions.consequences: Imports duplicate storage, visible in the library size view and covered by retention. Large video imports copy the whole file though only the audio track is used; extracting only the audio is a refinement once the cost is measured.
decisions.reconsider_when: Large video imports become common enough that storing extracted audio plus a bookmark beats keeping the original.

decisions.title: Speech runtime: WhisperKit ships, whisper.cpp is the designed second adapter
decisions.choice: Ship WhisperKit from the Argmax Swift package behind SpeechRecognizer, loaded inside the sandboxed speech service with an explicit local model folder and acquisition disabled. Keep whisper.cpp as a designed second adapter behind the same port, built when Intel coverage is required or if F1 or the notice inventory rules the first choice out.
decisions.rationale: Three pieces of evidence in RESEARCH support choosing now instead of deferring. The runtime is distributed as a Swift package and the stated build is SPM, so integration cost is lower than a C API that also needs its own decoding boundary. The WhisperKit model repository states MIT on its card, which is the only positive licensing evidence available for weights the application might offer for download. SpeakerKit ships in the same package, so the diarizer that Meetings requires arrives through one dependency and one acquisition path (D-023). What RESEARCH does not establish is accuracy, latency or long-recording behavior; those are measurements that evaluate the choice, defined by F1, and they are separate from the choice itself. The port keeps the decision reversible at the cost of one adapter.

alternatives.option: whisper.cpp as the shipping runtime
alternatives.tradeoff: Intel and Apple Silicon coverage today with widely available GGML weights; C interop in the hot path, an explicit decoding boundary its command-line example demands, and a second dependency and acquisition path for diarization.

alternatives.option: Maintain both runtimes permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility; two parameter translations, two evaluation runs per model update and two descriptor sets to keep current, paid before any evidence says both have a role.

alternatives.option: Defer the choice to a bake-off and build against the port only
alternatives.tradeoff: No commitment without measurement; leaves the model format, the acquisition path and the diarization dependency unsettled while capabilities that depend on them are designed.

alternatives.option: Apple's built-in speech recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: No models to manage; on-device availability and language coverage are controlled by the system and model choice is not exposed, which the requirements demand.

decisions.consequences: Intel is unsupported until the second adapter is built, and the shipped weights are in a format tied to Apple Silicon builds. Results record the runtime that produced them, so a change is visible in History. Until F1 completes, no accuracy or latency claim appears anywhere and the scheduler keeps cancel-and-restart preemption.
decisions.reconsider_when: F1 shows peak resident size growing with input duration in a way windowing cannot bound, the notice inventory blocks the weights the app would offer, or Intel becomes a requirement.

decisions.title: Generation runtime: llama.cpp embedded in the generation service, GGUF models
decisions.choice: Embed llama.cpp as a library in GenerationService, loading GGUF models with Metal on Apple Silicon and CPU otherwise, streaming tokens back over the connection. No server binary is used or shipped.
decisions.rationale: RESEARCH records llama.cpp as providing local inference with Metal support and as shipping both library integration material and server tooling, and asks that an embedded worker be compared with a local service including whether network access is possible. Embedding gives control over acquisition and lifecycle, and GGUF reaches the quantized models users already have, which matters because user-supplied models are in scope.

alternatives.option: MLX-based generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Apple-native with good Apple Silicon performance; a different model format, fewer ready quantizations and no Intel path.

alternatives.option: Core ML converted models
alternatives.tradeoff: System-managed execution and no vendored C++; per-model conversion work, and user-supplied models become impractical.

alternatives.option: The llama.cpp server on localhost
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses upstream tooling; the reachability and forwarding concerns in D-003 apply directly.

decisions.consequences: Vendored C++ with build time, pinning and update discipline. The service is built for target architectures and signed with the bundle. Quantization becomes a user-visible setting with a memory consequence surfaced through D-027.
decisions.reconsider_when: MLX coverage of the quantizations users bring becomes comparable, or measured generation latency on the target is unacceptable and another runtime measurably beats it.

decisions.title: Model identity, immutable content-addressed installs, transactional activation, recorded notices
decisions.choice: Identity is publisher name, revision string and a SHA-256 over the ordered weight file set. Installation stages into Models/.staging/<uuid>, verifies per-file and set hashes, runs a load smoke test in a service against the staged path, then renames the directory to Models/blobs/<setHash>, a path that never previously existed and is never written again; if that path already exists the content is already installed and staging is deleted. A single SQLite transaction then inserts the installation row, its per-asset rows with license identifier and retained notice, and updates the active pointer. Runs hold a lease on the installation they pinned. Garbage collection removes blobs with no installation row and no live lease, at launch and after lease release. Compatibility is checked before activation against the runtime descriptor: runtime kind, version range, quantization support, sample rate, context length. Quality scores never gate activation, and a compatible model with no benchmark row is fully usable and labeled unmeasured. Runtimes receive absolute paths and never load by name.
decisions.rationale: A sequence that spans a filesystem rename and a database update needs an ordering rule, and renaming over a live directory is not atomic. Immutable content-addressed blobs make installation idempotent and leave the only mutable state a database pointer that moves inside one transaction. Hashing weights instead of trusting a name makes the same model checkable across a rename or a re-download, and the smoke test catches the common user-supplied failure at install instead of mid-dictation. RESEARCH warns that a default runtime initialization may download models, so passing explicit paths is the enforcement point, and it asks that the license and revision of each selected model be preserved in the installation manifest, which is why notices are recorded per asset.

alternatives.option: Identity by file name or publisher identifier
alternatives.tradeoff: No hashing cost on multi-gigabyte files; two quantizations under one name become indistinguishable in History.

alternatives.option: Install in place and roll back on failure
alternatives.tradeoff: No staging space needed; a failure during the write leaves a corrupt live model, the outcome the requirement forbids.

alternatives.option: Versioned slots with an activation journal
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps old and new side by side without content addressing; recovery logic is more involved and duplicate content is stored twice.

alternatives.option: Let the runtime's own downloader manage models
alternatives.tradeoff: Much less code; hands acquisition to a component that may download implicitly, breaking the offline contract.

decisions.consequences: Installation needs free space for the staged and the stored copy, checked before starting. Hashing large files takes time and is shown as a verification step. Blobs can outlive their rows briefly after a crash and are collected at launch. Failed user imports stay in staging with the error attached until dismissed. Assets whose notice cannot be established are importable but never offered for download.
decisions.reconsider_when: Hashing time becomes a usability problem, which argues for incremental hashing during download, or lease contention patterns make a different pinning scheme preferable.

decisions.title: Meetings: SpeakerKit diarization with channel origin as fact and attribution as hypothesis
decisions.choice: Record microphone and system audio as separate artifacts with role recorded as a capture fact, aligned by host time, labeled as the microphone channel and the system audio channel in the interface. Diarize with SpeakerKit's Pyannote pipeline behind a Diarizer port, configured explicitly with download disabled, an explicit model folder and explicit segmenter and embedder concurrency, all recorded in the run manifest. Weights are user-acquired through the model store and never bundled. Each segment carries attribution_state in {assigned, unverified, assigned_by_user, unattributed}, cluster identity, and clustering distance and margin as evidence; calibrated confidence is stored as unknown when the runtime supplies none. Names attach to speaker_identities holding centroid embeddings; a later run matches by embedding similarity and weak matches are presented for confirmation. Segments correlating with delayed system audio are marked probable echo and excluded from microphone-side attribution. Notes are generated over the timestamped transcript in overlapping windows with per-bullet segment citations, and uncited bullets are dropped.
decisions.rationale: The requirement asks for speaker assignment, editable names and an explicit runtime choice, so the runtime is named now: it lives in the package already selected for speech, and RESEARCH documents the configuration flags that keep it from downloading. RESEARCH also states that the available clustering threshold is not evidence of a calibrated probability, so the design represents missing calibration as unknown and keeps a user path to assign or correct, which is what satisfies the requirement without claiming certainty. A microphone can pick up remote audio from speakers and a system stream can carry several applications, so channel origin is not identity. Cluster numbers are arbitrary across runs, so carrying user-edited names on numeric identity would misattribute silently after re-clustering.

alternatives.option: Diarize a single mixed recording
alternatives.tradeoff: One file and one capture path; discards the channel signal and makes even the easiest question an inference.

alternatives.option: Treat channels as speaker identity
alternatives.tradeoff: Labels users understand immediately; wrong whenever speakers leak into the microphone or several people share a room.

alternatives.option: Assign every segment to the nearest cluster
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean-looking transcripts; confidently wrong attributions in notes, the failure the requirements call out.

alternatives.option: Ship meetings with channel labels only until a diarizer is measured
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids shipping unmeasured attribution; drops a requested feature, so it is rejected as a resolution even though the measurement is still owed.

alternatives.option: Generate notes in one pass over the whole transcript
alternatives.tradeoff: Better global structure; exceeds context on long meetings and gives no way to check a bullet against the audio.

decisions.consequences: Two artifacts per meeting at native rate, roughly doubling meeting storage. Diarization weights are an explicit acquisition step the model manager shows, because notices for the embedder and clusterer are component-specific. Echo thresholds come from evaluation and not from this document. Dropping uncited bullets can remove a correct line that failed to cite, so the drop rate is tracked. Attribution shown as unverified is a normal state the transcript view must explain.
decisions.reconsider_when: Evaluation shows clustering distance is monotone with correctness, allowing a derived threshold with its calibration curve; a notice blocks integration, moving to another diarizer behind the same port; or mixed-stream diarization matches channel-separated results.

decisions.title: History: append-only results over identified runs, full-text search, tombstones with generation tokens
decisions.choice: History lists recordings, each expandable into its processing runs and their result chains. Search is FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets. Playback uses the sealed artifact. Reprocessing creates a run and inserts results; nothing is mutated, and a user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter and signals cancellation; every worker carries recording id and generation from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned or at a different generation. Hard deletion happens when the last lease releases or at the next launch sweep.
decisions.rationale: A late worker response cannot recreate a deleted recording only if the existence check and the insert are the same transaction; any check-then-insert has a window. The generation counter covers delete-then-recreate at the same identifier. Organizing the list by run is what makes reprocessing through a different speech model comparable instead of confusing, since each run names the models and mode revision that produced its chain.

alternatives.option: Hard delete immediately and let workers fail
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone bookkeeping; a constraint violation becomes the race outcome and scratch files are orphaned.

alternatives.option: Cancel workers and wait for acknowledgement before deleting
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone state; the user's delete blocks on a worker mid-window, and a hung worker blocks it indefinitely.

alternatives.option: Overwrite results on reprocessing
alternatives.tradeoff: One result per recording and a simpler list; comparing a new model against the old becomes impossible, which is a stated use of reprocessing.

decisions.consequences: Deleted recordings hold disk until leases release, so the interface says deleting instead of claiming reclaimed space. FTS triggers must handle result deletion, covered by tests. A recording with several runs needs a detail view that makes each run's recognition and current result obvious at a glance.
decisions.reconsider_when: Result rows dominate database size, which argues for storing older results compressed or on disk instead of inline.

decisions.title: Desktop behavior: menu bar surface, software input gain, media pause with manual resume
decisions.choice: An NSStatusItem shows state, current mode, recent results and settings. Microphone level is software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in. Media pausing checks whether the default output device is running before capture and posts a play-pause key when it is. Resume is a user action offered in the panel and menu for ten minutes after recording. Automatic resume is opt-in and fires only if the app posted the pause, the same output device is still default, the device is still idle and under ten minutes have elapsed. Device volume is restored only if the current value still equals the value the app set.
decisions.rationale: The app can observe that some client is running on the output device and can post a media key; neither identifies the application that reacted or confirms that anything paused. Automatic resume built on that evidence can start playback the user stopped by hand. Offering resume as an action keeps the convenience while removing the wrong-action failure, and users who accept the risk can enable automatic resume with its conditions stated. Software gain changes no system setting, so the default has no restore obligation at all.

alternatives.option: Automatic resume on by default under the ownership conditions
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to click after recording; the conditions cannot establish which application received the key, so it can resume something the user stopped deliberately.

alternatives.option: Private MediaRemote framework for playback state and control
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate per-application state and precise control; an undocumented interface that can break on any OS update and complicates notarization posture.

alternatives.option: Per-application scripting for known players
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise for a short list of players; needs automation permission per application and covers only that list.

alternatives.option: Do not touch media playback
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to get wrong; leaves background audio bleeding into recordings, which the requirement asks to address.

decisions.consequences: Users get a Resume control instead of automatic restoration unless they opt in, and the menu states that the app cannot confirm which application it addressed. Software gain cannot rescue a signal clipped at the hardware, which the clipping indicator surfaces so the user can lower device gain.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API supplies target identity and confirms the pause transition, at which point automatic resume can become the default for confirmed targets.

decisions.title: Shortcuts: distinct toggle and push-to-talk bindings, evidence-based stuck-key recovery, no duration cap
decisions.choice: A single ShortcutRegistrar owns a session-level consuming CGEventTap handling keyDown, keyUp and flagsChanged. Toggle and push-to-talk are separate bindings; a combination may be bound to at most one of them, validated at bind time. Toggle acts on keyDown and ignores keyUp. Push-to-talk starts on keyDown and finalizes on keyUp, with an optional per-binding tap-to-lock where a keyUp within a configurable window, 250 ms by default, latches recording until the next press. Lost key-up is recovered from evidence: tap-disabled notifications, screen lock and sleep notifications, and a 1 Hz poll of the physical key state that finalizes when the key reports up while the app believes it is down. There is no maximum recording duration. Per-mode bindings are toggle or push-to-talk bindings with a mode attached. kCGEventTapDisabledByTimeout re-enables the tap. Without the tap, toggle falls back to Carbon RegisterEventHotKey and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation.
decisions.rationale: Overloading one binding with a hold discriminator leaves the first hold window undefined and makes a short press ambiguous. Separate bindings remove the ambiguity. Polling the physical key state addresses the real problem, a key-up the tap never delivered, with evidence about that key, while a maximum-hold watchdog would truncate valid speech and act as the recording-duration limit the specification prohibits.

alternatives.option: One binding with a hold discriminator
alternatives.tradeoff: One combination to configure; the first hold window has undefined behavior and a dropped event changes the meaning of a press.

alternatives.option: Carbon RegisterEventHotKey only
alternatives.tradeoff: No Accessibility permission and reliable consumption; no key-up, so push-to-talk cannot exist.

alternatives.option: NSEvent global monitors only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple API with no tap lifecycle; events cannot be consumed, so the hotkey also reaches the foreground application.

alternatives.option: A maximum hold watchdog
alternatives.tradeoff: Guarantees a stuck key eventually stops recording; truncates a genuinely long push-to-talk recording, which the specification forbids.

decisions.consequences: The app sits on the keyboard event path, so its handler must stay fast or the tap is disabled by timeout, which the re-enable path treats as a monitored condition. Users configure two shortcuts instead of one. The key-state poll runs only while a push-to-talk recording is active.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API provides global hotkeys with key-up, or the poll proves unreliable for remapped or external keyboards, which would argue for a visible stuck-key banner with a stop control.

decisions.title: Model residency under a declared budget that measurement replaces
decisions.choice: Budget the application at 8 GB peak on the 16 GB target, counting the app and its services. At most one speech and one generation model resident, unloaded after ten idle minutes. Activation of a pairing whose footprint exceeds the budget is refused with the arithmetic shown, the refusal stating whether its numbers are measured or declared, and an explicit override available. Once F1 descriptors exist, admission uses measured peak resident size and Metal heap peak per installation instead of declared file sizes.
decisions.rationale: The specification forbids artificial quotas and requires honest reporting of limits, which differs from ignoring the ceiling: swap on a 16 GB machine turns a latency problem into a system-wide stall. Declared weight sizes omit runtime workspaces, Metal allocations and service overhead, so a refusal computed from them can deny a pairing that would have worked. Labeling the basis and keeping the override means the policy never becomes a limit the user cannot see through.

alternatives.option: Load on demand with no residency limit
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fastest where memory allows; on the stated target a large pairing plus a browser drives the machine into swap.

alternatives.option: Keep selected models resident permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest per-run latency; several gigabytes held while the app idles in the menu bar.

alternatives.option: Rely on memory pressure notifications alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to real conditions; reacts after the stall has started.

decisions.consequences: First use after idle pays a model load shown as a loading state. Until descriptors exist the budget is arithmetic that can be wrong in either direction, which the refusal text says. Memory pressure notifications still trigger early unload of idle models.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured residency differs materially from declared sizes, or the app runs on machines where the ceiling does not bind.

decisions.title: Egress control enforced by the service sandbox
decisions.choice: Inference and decoding run in services whose sandbox omits the network client entitlement, so the system denies outbound connections. Downloads happen only through ModelDownloader on explicit user action, restricted to an allowlist of model hosts and writing only into staging. Runtimes receive absolute local paths, are constructed with acquisition disabled, and a static check fails the build if a runtime is constructed through an initializer that can download. The external decoder runs as a child of the sandboxed decode service, is off by default, and is disabled entirely by the strict offline setting. The product claim is that inference and decoding run in processes the system denies network access, evidenced by an in-service connection attempt that fails, with build checks and a network-denied session as secondary evidence.
decisions.rationale: The specification requires that audio, transcripts and context stay on the Mac and that model loading not trigger downloads, and RESEARCH notes a diarization runtime whose default initialization may download models. RESEARCH also states that a scan for socket symbols cannot establish that a process lacks network access and points at signed services with entitlements withheld as the thing to evaluate. An entitlement is a property of the process, so it covers linked frameworks and dynamically loaded code that no scan reaches.

alternatives.option: Symbol scan plus a network-denied session test only
alternatives.tradeoff: No platform dependency and no entitlement work; cannot cover system frameworks or dynamically loaded code, and RESEARCH rejects the scan as evidence of absence.

alternatives.option: Allow runtimes to fetch missing models
alternatives.tradeoff: Better first run with no model manager; makes network access a side effect of loading a model, which the requirements forbid.

alternatives.option: Ship no downloader and require manual placement
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee and least code; makes first run considerably harder and pushes users toward downloading models through less careful means.

alternatives.option: Remove the external decoder entirely
alternatives.tradeoff: No user-selected binary at all; users with opus in matroska have no path until a decoder is bundled, and the specification asks for an extension mechanism.

decisions.consequences: Entitlement sets become part of the signed product, and a missing one fails closed. The model access path depends on F2, since a sandboxed service needs descriptors or a path exception to read weights. The decoder is constrained only if sandbox inheritance holds; if it does not, the decoder stays off by default with the trust transfer stated in its settings.
decisions.reconsider_when: F2 shows the sandbox blocks model loading for the chosen runtimes, or shows that a spawned decoder does not inherit the restriction.

decisions.title: Processing runs as the provenance spine of every derived artifact
decisions.choice: processing_runs sits between recordings and results. Every result belongs to a run and names its immediate input through derived_from_result_id; recognition results are chain roots and carry the speech model installation that produced them. A recording may hold several recognition results, one per recognition run. Results are immutable after insert, enforced by a trigger.
decisions.rationale: A recording cannot have exactly one source transcript while also being re-recognizable through a different speech model. After a second recognition, a translation or rewrite would have no way to say which words it came from, and an invariant that the source transcript is never mutated would hide a replacement behind a supposedly unique row. Making the run the unit that pins settings and owns a chain answers provenance with a foreign key instead of with inference.

alternatives.option: Keep one transcript per recording and forbid re-recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: The simplest graph and the shortest History view; removes reprocessing through another speech model, which the requirements ask for.

alternatives.option: Version the transcript in place with a revision counter
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer rows than runs; older derived results end up pointing at a version that no longer matches the displayed text.

alternatives.option: Attach model ids to results and infer parentage by timestamp
alternatives.tradeoff: No new table; parentage becomes a guess that breaks whenever two runs overlap, which the batch lane makes routine.

decisions.consequences: More joins in History queries and a detail view that presents runs instead of a flat result list. Reprocessing gains a clear entry stage, since a text reprocess names its parent result and skips recognition. The FTS index carries results from every run, so search can return two recognitions of the same audio, which the result rows disambiguate.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users never re-recognize, which would make the run table pure overhead, though the same structure is what makes translations and notes attributable.

decisions.title: Crash-safe capture through an fsynced chunk journal with incremental sealing
decisions.choice: Capture writes fixed-period chunks, two seconds by default, of headerless native-rate PCM, each written to a part file, fsynced, renamed, with the directory fsynced. A sealer encodes completed chunks into the ALAC artifact, appends chunk, packet and offset entries to an fsynced index, and deletes chunks it has durably encoded. At capture end the packet table is written from the index and the artifact is fsynced and hashed. Recovery rebuilds the packet table from the index, truncates to the last durable extent, and appends surviving chunks.
decisions.rationale: Asserting that a partially written ALAC-in-CAF file can be finalized after SIGKILL would make the recovery contract depend on an untested property of a container that stores its packet table at the end. Recovery here depends only on records the application writes and fsyncs itself. Worst-case loss is the unsealed tail, bounded by the chunk period plus unflushed data within it, and the exact figure comes from the kill-at-offset experiment.

alternatives.option: Write the container directly and rely on it being recoverable
alternatives.tradeoff: No journal, no sealer, no extra fsyncs; the recovery story rests on an untested property of the container format.

alternatives.option: Keep raw PCM as the only durable form until the run completes
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest recovery; transient storage equals the full raw recording, which for a three-hour two-stream meeting is several gigabytes.

alternatives.option: Write a second copy of the container periodically
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovery reads the last complete copy; doubles write volume and still loses everything since the last copy.

decisions.consequences: An fsync every chunk period and a sealer to maintain, plus roughly a 30-second window of journal files alongside the artifact during long captures. Chunk period is the tuning knob between recovery loss and write frequency. Sealing is idempotent, which is what makes recovery from the sealing state safe.
decisions.reconsider_when: The kill-at-offset experiment shows a loss bound the product cannot live with, or a container format with an incrementally durable index removes the need for a separate journal.

decisions.title: A state-indexed recovery contract with an explicit durability ordering rule
decisions.choice: Every non-terminal run state has an authoritative recovery transition, listed in the data lifecycle, and the ordering rule is written down: a durable record of intent precedes an externally visible irreversible effect, while a locally idempotent effect is followed by its commit. Recovery may complete deterministic stages such as refining, and never resumes generation or delivery without user action.
decisions.rationale: A recovery sweep that covers only some states leaves the rest to whichever test author reaches them first, which is the deferral the specification prohibits. Naming the ordering rule also makes new stages easy to place correctly instead of case by case.

alternatives.option: Discard any run that was in flight at a crash
alternatives.tradeoff: One rule and no partial state; throws away a completed recognition because the app crashed during a rewrite.

alternatives.option: Resume every in-flight run automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Least user friction; re-runs generation the user may no longer want and risks re-delivering into whatever is now focused.

alternatives.option: Ask the user at launch what to do with each interrupted run
alternatives.tradeoff: No wrong default; a dialog listing interrupted work at every launch after a crash is a poor first impression and invites blind dismissal.

decisions.consequences: Recovery does deterministic work automatically and stops at anything that consumes a model or touches another application. Behavior tables must cover every state, and the crash-injection suite asserts against them instead of against improvised expectations.
decisions.reconsider_when: A new stage appears whose effects are neither externally visible nor idempotent, which would need a rule of its own instead of a case in this table.

decisions.title: Permissions as a capability-by-state matrix
decisions.choice: A matrix over capability, run state and active adapter replaces any single revocation outcome. Losing microphone or an active system-audio stream terminates capture; losing Accessibility affects insertion and shortcut consumption and not recognition; losing Input Monitoring affects shortcuts; losing browser automation affects URL predicates; losing Screen Recording ends screen context and system-audio capture while leaving microphone capture running. Denial at launch, revocation during work and restoration each have a defined effect, and restoration is reported once.
decisions.rationale: Mapping every revocation to a capture failure would end a valid recording because the user changed a delivery permission during recognition, and would report a lost shortcut permission as an audio failure. Capabilities serve different stages, so their loss belongs at those stages.

alternatives.option: One global failure state
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to implement and explain; stops work that is still valid and misreports the cause.

alternatives.option: Ignore revocation until the capability is next used
alternatives.tradeoff: No mid-run interruption; the user gets a confusing failure later with no connection to the change they made.

decisions.consequences: The matrix is longer than a rule, is directly testable, and becomes part of the approved behavior tables. Each capability needs a probe and a change notification path.
decisions.reconsider_when: A capability appears whose loss affects several stages differently enough that the matrix needs a third dimension beyond adapter identity.

decisions.title: One artifact lease protocol shared by workers, playback, export and retention
decisions.choice: A leases table records holder, artifact, acquisition and heartbeat. Acquiring a lease requires the recording row to exist, be untombstoned and match the expected generation. Workers, the audio player, exports and every retention policy acquire leases. Retention skips recordings with a live lease and retries on the next pass. Discarding audio is a distinct audio_discarded state that disables playback and re-recognition while leaving text reprocessing available. Stale leases are reclaimed at launch and by a sweeper.
decisions.rationale: Giving user-initiated deletion a tombstone and generation protocol while letting age, size and audio-only policies bypass it would let a scheduled policy remove an artifact under an admitted job or during playback, and leave History offering playback that no longer works. One protocol for every consumer removes the class of race instead of one instance.

alternatives.option: Retention as immediate deletion with best-effort cancellation
alternatives.tradeoff: Policies always run on schedule; a race with an admitted job produces a failure whose outcome depends on timing.

alternatives.option: Quiesce all work before retention runs
alternatives.tradeoff: No leases needed; a long import blocks retention indefinitely, and retention blocks new work while it runs.

alternatives.option: Reference counting in memory only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper than a table; counts vanish on a crash, so recovery cannot tell which artifacts were in use.

decisions.consequences: Every consumer of an artifact acquires and heartbeats a lease, including playback, which is more ceremony than a player usually needs. Retention can lag when a recording stays busy, which is reported instead of forced. Lease reclamation is part of the launch sweep.
decisions.reconsider_when: Lease contention delays retention long enough to matter, which would argue for pausing playback and preempting batch work in place of deferring.

decisions.title: Measurements precede the boundaries they can invalidate; task phases follow acceptance
decisions.choice: Four evidence gates (F1 runtime harness, F2 service isolation, F3 kill-at-offset capture, F4 insertion matrix) run before the boundaries that depend on them, as described under evolution. The design records ordering constraints, dependencies and acceptance evidence per capability area; the task-level phase breakdown is produced after this design is accepted.
decisions.rationale: Four decisions here depend on properties nothing has measured: how the chosen runtime behaves on long input and under cancellation, whether a sandboxed service can load models and is denied the network, how much audio a crash costs, and which applications allow confirmable insertion. Scheduling those after the ports and schema that depend on them would mean a negative result invalidates work already built on it. Each gate has a fallback that satisfies the requirement it touches, so a negative result changes a parameter or an adapter and not the architecture.

alternatives.option: Start the skeleton immediately and measure later
alternatives.tradeoff: Visible progress sooner; a negative F1 or F3 result forces rework of the ingest port, the scheduler and the capture writer.

alternatives.option: Prototype everything end to end before designing
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum evidence before commitment; delays every requirement that does not depend on the unknowns.

alternatives.option: Treat the unknowns as risks accepted at implementation time
alternatives.tradeoff: No gates to schedule; hands behavioral decisions to whichever task hits them, which the specification forbids.

decisions.consequences: Some work produces evidence instead of shippable behavior: descriptors, matrices, bounds and decision updates. Gate outputs feed D-001, D-004, D-009, D-020, D-027, D-028 and D-030, so those decisions carry conservative defaults until the evidence lands.
decisions.reconsider_when: A gate's fallback proves acceptable enough that the measurement is not worth its cost, which is a judgment to record instead of assume.

decisions.title: Named approval authority and specification traceability for expected behavior
decisions.choice: Expected behavior lives in docs/behavior/ tables whose rows each cite a SPEC.md clause or are marked derived. The normative approver is the user as product owner, or a delegate named in docs/behavior/OWNERS. Approval of a table gates writing tests against it; tests reference row identifiers; changing an approved row requires re-approval recorded in git history. Independent authorship of tables is a hygiene rule and carries no authority.
decisions.rationale: A passing test proves only that the code met its assertions, so the assertions need an owner who can say they are the intended product behavior. Requiring review by someone other than the author establishes neither product authority nor fidelity to the specification. Clause citations make it possible to check that a requirement was followed into the design instead of paraphrased.

alternatives.option: Peer review by any team member
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and fast; two people can share the same misreading of a requirement with nobody empowered to settle it.

alternatives.option: Treat SPEC.md as the only source and skip behavior tables
alternatives.tradeoff: No second artifact to maintain; the specification does not enumerate state and event pairs, so implementers fill the gaps silently.

alternatives.option: Derive expectations from the implementation and review the diff
alternatives.tradeoff: Least documentation work; makes the code its own specification, which is the failure this decision exists to prevent.

decisions.consequences: Capability areas cannot be accepted until their tables are approved, which puts the product owner on the critical path. Derived rows are visible as a category, so the volume of behavior with no specification basis stays measurable.
decisions.reconsider_when: Approval becomes the dominant delay, which would argue for pre-approved templates for mechanical tables instead of removing the gate.

coverage.explanation: Global toggle and push-to-talk from another application come from one session-level event tap that observes key-up and consumes the hotkey (D-026). Toggle and push-to-talk are separate configurable bindings, so a press has one meaning and no hold window is ambiguous; per-mode bindings select a mode and start a run in one action, with in-app conflict detection at bind time and a test-press step for system conflicts. A lost key-up is recovered from tap-disabled and screen-lock notifications and from polling the physical key state, so there is no maximum hold and no recording-duration cap. Without Accessibility or Input Monitoring the tap cannot run, so toggle falls back to a Carbon hotkey and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation instead of failing silently (D-032). Cancellation has a defined effect at every stage (D-007) because stages are explicit run states (D-006): arming discards, capturing discards the journal by default, recognizing keeps audio and saves no partial transcript, refining drops the normalized result, rewriting keeps it and offers it, and delivering is cancellable only before the first event is posted. A crash mid-run resolves through the state-indexed recovery contract (D-031).

The processed transcript is inserted at the caret or over the current selection by setting AXSelectedText; the app never sets an element's whole value, so existing field contents survive (D-009), which follows the distinction RESEARCH draws between an accessibility object's value and its selected text. Where that path is unavailable, the pasteboard path posts Command-V and reads the target's state back when it is readable, treating an observed change as delivered and an observed absence as rejected; synthesized typing is attempted only after an observed rejection, and a target with no readable state gets one unconfirmed attempt and no retry, because posting a paste event carries no acknowledgment. Optional submission uses the modifier sampled at stop and posts Return only when delivery reached the latched element through a path that posted events. The target is latched at arming with its insertion capability, and focus changes have explicit outcomes: same element delivers, same application with a different element delivers by default, another application holds with Deliver and Copy, a departed application holds (D-008). Clipboard changes are handled by snapshotting before writing and restoring after the outcome is known, only while the change count is ours, deferred for unconfirmed outcomes and skipped for targets that read late or content that cannot be snapshotted, with the user told before anything is written. Permissions denied or revoked route the result to History and the pasteboard through the capability matrix instead of ending the run (D-032), and secure input suppresses synthesis entirely. Duplicate delivery is prevented structurally: the attempt row commits before any event is posted, and pending, posted and unconfirmed attempts become needs_review at launch and are never re-posted (D-010).

A provisional live transcript comes from a separate pass over a sliding window and a waveform is drawn from a 10 ms RMS and peak envelope computed allocation-free on the capture thread (D-011). The compact window is a non-activating, borderless panel at status-bar level that joins all spaces, is movable by its background and never becomes key, so showing it cannot break the delivery latch. Placement is remembered as a fraction of the display's visible frame plus the display identifier and is clamped to the primary display when either is gone. Provisional text renders in a secondary style with a live label and is replaced by the final transcript with a change highlight; the provisional stream is never persisted as a result, because it was produced over partial context and is a different artifact from the recognition result the run commits (D-006). Recording and processing failures appear as a panel row with a short reason and one action, including the case where the scheduler declines the provisional pass while batch work holds the speech model, which shows as preview paused (D-004). Whether the provisional pass can run without costing dropped buffers or final quality is a measurement listed under verification, and the degraded presentation already has a defined state.

Four built-in modes cover ordinary dictation and task-specific output: Standard, Email, Note and Meeting notes (D-013). Each carries a structured transformation contract instead of a prose description. Standard is limited to punctuation, capitalization, optional disfluency removal and vocabulary substitution; Email adds template salutation and sign-off, paragraph structure and register adjustment with no new factual content; Note adds list and heading structure; Meeting notes permits summarization because that is its purpose and is bounded by a citation requirement in place of a recall threshold. All four declare that they do not answer questions, and the validator enforces that interrogatives in the normalized transcript survive in order, that expansion stays within the mode's limit, that content-word recall clears the threshold, and that no long span appears which is present in the context block and absent from the transcript (D-012). A failure retries once with a stricter instruction and then falls back to the normalized transcript, marked as a validator fallback. In a language with no validator pack for the mode, the generation stage is skipped and the normalized transcript is used, so the prohibition on answering never rests on an unenforced check. A mode that answered dictated questions would have to declare that in its contract, which also makes it visibly distinct in the mode indicator.

Users author prompts and formatting rules, and each custom mode also fills in a structured transformation contract naming its allowed operations, whether it may answer questions, its content bound and the languages its validator supports; the editor cannot save a mode without one, because a free-form prompt gives the validator nothing to check against (D-012). Each mode selects its own local speech and language models by content identity instead of by name (D-022). Every save creates a content-addressed revision in an append-only chain, and every run pins the revision id into its manifest at start along with model installations, vocabulary revision, language and validator pack (D-006). Work already in progress reads its snapshot and never live settings, so editing a mode or switching models during a recognition cannot change what the running job produces. Saved results keep pointing at the revision that produced them, and History names that revision and diffs it against the current one, so a later edit cannot silently change the meaning of an earlier result. Because every result also names the run and the parent result it derives from (D-029), a rewrite produced by an old revision stays attributable even after the audio is recognized again under a different model.

Rules match the foreground application's bundle identifier and, where readable, the website URL, evaluated once at arming with first match winning over a user-ordered list (D-014). Conflicts resolve by that order, with specificity as the tiebreak within equal priority, and the editor flags rules that can never fire because an earlier rule shadows them. When a predicate's input cannot be obtained, because browser automation is denied, the browser exposes no URL, or screen recording is off, rules needing that input do not match and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies. Permission loss is handled per capability, so losing browser automation narrows rule matching without disturbing capture or recognition (D-032). The chosen mode is latched into the run manifest, so it cannot change mid-sentence, and the effective mode plus whether it came from a rule or the fallback appears in the recording panel and the menu bar for every run, which is what keeps the current mode apparent (D-011). Which browsers expose a URL is enumerated in a dated matrix before URL rules ship instead of assumed, and an incomplete matrix degrades to bundle-identifier rules.

User terminology and names enter at four points with a fixed order relative to recognition and language processing (D-015). Before recognition, selected terms go into the decoder's prompt slot, bounded by the runtime's limit and chosen by mode relevance and recency; that shifts decoding probabilities and the interface says exactly that, with no claim that adding a name guarantees recognition, because the mechanism is a prompt and not a decoding constraint (D-020). After recognition, configurable replacements run deterministically over the recognition result with longest-match-first, boundary-aware, case-preserving, non-overlapping, single-pass semantics, using ICU word segmentation for the run's language and falling back to substring matching with a warning where segmentation is unavailable. Filler removal is a separate per-mode pass after replacement. After generation the replacement table is applied once more and the validator checks that vocabulary terms survived (D-012), because a language model will sometimes normalize an unusual proper noun back to a common word and the user's spelling should win. Recognition and normalized results are both retained, so the effect of each stage is inspectable, and where no validator pack exists the run takes the fail-closed path and delivers the normalized text with its replacements applied.

Three optional sources are sampled at arming in parallel against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text, selection and window title through accessibility; one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition when opted in; and the first text item on the pasteboard, each capped (D-016). Sampling once at arming bounds cost and makes a run reproducible; anything missing the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Retention defaults to a digest, byte length and source kind instead of the text, so the library does not accumulate copies of unrelated documents and screens, while a later reprocess can still report that the original context is unavailable; retaining text is opt-in per mode, shown in History and deleted with the recording. Missing permissions leave a named operating state: no Screen Recording means no screen context and no system audio while everything else continues, and losing Accessibility removes focused-element context without ending an in-flight run (D-032). Context is supplied as data, fenced in a per-run random delimiter and labeled reference material with mode instructions before it and the task restated after. Framing alone does not constrain a model, so the requirement that context must not override processing instructions is carried by the contract validator, including the check that rejects any span of eight or more tokens present in the context and absent from the transcript, with the fail-closed fallback to the normalized transcript when validation is unavailable (D-012). Context never leaves the machine: it crosses only an XPC connection to a service the system denies network access (D-028).

Recognition language is set per mode to an explicit code or to detection using the runtime's language identification with its probability; below the threshold the run records undetermined, uses the mode's default and the panel says so (D-017). Translation into English is a separate declared operation that inserts a result naming the exact recognition or normalized result it translated, so the source transcript is preserved beside any derived text and stays identifiable even after the same audio is recognized again under a different model (D-029). Recognition and rewriting are evaluated by different methods and reported separately, word error rate for the first and a human rubric for the second, because a rewrite score cannot distinguish a mis-recognized word from a badly reworded sentence. Compatibility is declared per model installation and checked against the runtime descriptor at activation (D-022); the interface attributes language claims to the model publisher and marks them unmeasured until an evaluation row exists, so no coverage is promised on documentation alone. Rewriting is additionally limited by validator pack coverage: a mode and language pair with no pack takes the fail-closed path and delivers the normalized transcript unless the user sets a per-mode override that is recorded on the result (D-012), so multilingual recognition is broader than multilingual rewriting and the interface states which.

Microphone, system audio and imported audio and video all implement one AudioSource that emits native-format frames carrying stream id, clock domain, presentation time, sequence and a discontinuity flag, with conversion to the canonical 16 kHz mono recognition input as an explicit stage after the port (D-018). Consumers grant credit, so a seekable source stops decoding when the recognizer falls behind and a live source that overruns records a discontinuity instead of buffering without bound; credit extends across the service connection, which is what bounds memory in both processes instead of in the decoder alone. The initial format matrix is what the system decoders cover: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v and mov. The extension mechanism is a DecoderProvider port with an opt-in external command-line decoder, off by default, run as a child of the sandboxed decode service so it inherits the same restrictions if inheritance holds and is otherwise carried as a stated trust transfer (D-028). Files decode in 30-second windows, and the memory claim is tested as a slope across 10-minute, 1-hour and 3-hour imports measured in both the app and the speech service, since a single run in one process cannot establish independence from duration. A failed import leaves its source unchanged because the path opens it read-only, copies into the session directory, and commits only after the artifact is complete; on failure the directory is removed and no row exists (D-019). Imports run in the batch lane and yield to interactive dictation under the scheduler's preemption policy for the runtime in use (D-004).

A meeting captures microphone and system audio as two artifacts whose frames carry host-time stamps, so alignment and gaps are represented by the ingest port instead of reconstructed afterwards (D-018). Channel origin is recorded as a fact about capture and labeled as the microphone channel and the system audio channel; it is not presented as speaker identity, because a microphone can pick up remote audio from speakers and a system stream can carry several applications (D-023). Speaker separation has an explicit runtime: SpeakerKit's Pyannote pipeline behind a Diarizer port, configured with download disabled, an explicit model folder and explicit segmenter and embedder concurrency recorded in the manifest, with weights acquired by the user and never bundled. Segments carry an attribution state and evidence, and calibrated confidence is stored as unknown when the runtime supplies none, so a weak label appears as unverified and the user can assign, merge or split speakers by hand; manual assignment wins over any later run. Editing speaker names writes to identities holding centroid embeddings, so a rename never alters model output and a later diarization run matches identities by embedding similarity with confirmation for weak matches, instead of by cluster numbers that are arbitrary across runs. Timestamped notes are generated locally over the transcript in overlapping windows sized to the language model's context, each bullet citing a segment range and uncited bullets dropped, under the residency budget so a long meeting does not drive the machine into swap (D-027). Capture is crash-safe through the chunk journal, so an interrupted meeting yields a sealed artifact per stream with a bounded tail loss (D-030). Evaluation methods are named under verification and remain unperformed, so no attribution quality is claimed.

Recordings are searchable through FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets, and playable from the sealed artifact (D-005, D-024). Each recording expands into its processing runs, and each run into a result chain rooted at that run's recognition result, so reprocessing through another model or mode inserts a new run and new results while every earlier result stays immutable and attributable (D-029). The relationship between original audio and successive results is one recording to many runs to many results, with each result naming its immediate input, the mode revision and the model installations that produced it, which is what lets History compare two recognitions of the same audio without ambiguity. A user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion while processing is active sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter and signals cancellation; every worker carries the recording id and generation from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned or at a different generation, so a late response cannot recreate a deleted recording because the check and the insert cannot be separated. Retention is not a separate mechanism: age, size and audio-discarding policies acquire the same leases, skip recordings held by a worker or a player, and move audio to a distinct discarded state that disables playback and re-recognition while leaving text reprocessing available (D-033). Interrupted work resolves through the state-indexed recovery contract, so a crash during recognition or rewriting leaves committed results intact and offers a new run (D-031). Space is reported as deleting until the last lease releases.
